title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
directAnswer: This is plain level-order BFS plus a direction flag that flips every level. Always traverse the tree the same way (left-to-right, enqueuing children normally); only the ORDER you record each level alternates. The clean implementation collects each level into a deque and either appends to the back (left-to-right rows) or pushes to the front (right-to-left rows), so you never touch the actual traversal — just where each value lands in the row.

remember.pattern: Level-order BFS + per-level direction flag, insert front/back
remember.formula:
leftToRight = true
while queue:
    size = len(queue)
    row = deque()
    for i in range(size):
        node = queue.popleft()
        if leftToRight: row.append(node.val)   # back
        else:           row.appendleft(node.val)# front
        enqueue node.left, node.right (always normally)
    result.append(list(row))
    leftToRight = not leftToRight
rules: Keep the **traversal identical** every level — only the *recording order* flips.
Use a **deque per level**: append to the back on left-to-right rows, push to the front on right-to-left rows.
Toggle the direction flag **once per level**, after finishing the row — not per node.
Always enqueue children **left then right**; reversing enqueue order corrupts the next level's nodes.
Snapshot the queue **size** before the inner loop, exactly as in any level-order BFS.
whenToUse: Level-order output where alternate levels are reversed (serpentine / boustrophedon)
You need rows top-to-bottom but with flipping within-row order
Any 'snake' or 'zigzag' rendering of a tree by level
BFS is natural and you just need to control insertion order per row
antiSignals: Plain left-to-right rows → Level Order Traversal (no flag)
Only a per-level aggregate, not the full row → Average/Max of Levels
Only the last node of each level → Right Side View
Order across levels (not within) matters → that's bottom-up Level Order II
remember.takeaway: Zigzag is Level Order Traversal with one boolean. The insight that you should flip the *recording* order, never the *traversal* order, keeps the children-enqueue logic untouched and the code bug-free. Deque-front-insertion turns the reversal into an O(1)-per-node operation instead of reversing rows afterward.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you separate the traversal from the output ordering — flipping how each row is recorded with a direction flag rather than altering the BFS or reversing children, which is where candidates introduce bugs.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reversing the order children are enqueued (which scrambles subsequent levels), or reversing the row list with O(width) work each time instead of inserting at the front of a deque.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State 'traversal stays constant, only recording order flips', use a deque for O(1) front insertion, and note the alternative of building normally then reversing odd rows — explaining the small efficiency difference.

problemStatement: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **zigzag level order traversal** of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between).
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 2000]
Output is a list of lists, one per level, with alternating within-row direction
understanding: We still visit the tree level by level, top to bottom — that part is identical to ordinary level-order traversal. The only twist is the within-row ordering: level 0 reads left-to-right, level 1 right-to-left, level 2 left-to-right again, and so on. Critically, the tree's structure and the parent-child links never change; only the direction in which we lay out each row's values alternates.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the zigzag affect how I traverse, or only how I output?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only the output. You traverse identically every level and merely reverse the recording order on alternate levels. Changing the traversal itself is the classic mistake.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which direction does the first (root) level go?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Left to right. So even-indexed levels (0, 2, 4, …) are left-to-right and odd-indexed levels are right-to-left.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the range starts at 0. A null root returns an empty list of levels.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I reverse children when enqueuing to flip a level?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — that corrupts the order of grandchildren. Always enqueue left then right; flip only where each value is placed in the row.

approaches.name: Level-Order BFS with a Direction Flag and Deque Insertion (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Frame it as 'ordinary level order, but a boolean controls whether each row is filled front or back'.
hints: Strip away the zigzag for a second: this is level-order traversal. What's the minimal change to flip the order of every other level?
Keep a boolean leftToRight that toggles after each level. Don't change how you traverse — change where you place each node's value in the row.
Use a deque for the current row: when going left-to-right, add to the back; when right-to-left, add to the front. Each insertion is O(1), so no row reversal is needed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once, and each value is inserted into a deque in O(1) (front or back) → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level (width w) and the output stores all n values → O(n) space overall.
approaches.explanation:
The cleanest way to think about zigzag is to realize that **the traversal never changes — only the presentation does**. We run exactly the same breadth-first, level-by-level sweep as ordinary level-order traversal, enqueuing each node's children left-then-right every single time. The 'zigzag' lives purely in how we *record* each level's values into the output.

**Why a direction flag is all you need.** We keep a boolean `leftToRight`, true for the root's level. After finishing each level we flip it. While filling a level, the flag decides *where in the row* the current node's value goes. On a left-to-right level we append to the back (natural order); on a right-to-left level we push to the front, so the first node visited ends up last in the row — achieving the reversal without ever changing the order in which we *visit* nodes.

**Why a deque makes this O(1) per node.** Reversing a list of width `w` afterward costs `O(w)`. Instead, we collect each level into a double-ended queue: `append` to the back for left-to-right, `appendleft` (push front) for right-to-left. Front insertion on a deque is `O(1)`, so the whole row is built in `O(w)` regardless of direction, with no separate reversal pass. At the end of the level we convert the deque to a plain list and add it to the result.

**Why we must NOT reverse the child-enqueue order.** A tempting but broken idea is to enqueue children right-then-left on alternate levels to 'naturally' flip the next row. This corrupts everything below: the order of a level's nodes determines the order their children are dequeued, so flipping enqueue order on one level scrambles the grandchildren's order in a way that compounds. By keeping enqueue order fixed (left then right, always) and isolating the flip to the recording step, the BFS frontier stays correct and only the output is serpentine.

**Why the size snapshot still matters.** As in any level-order BFS, we read `size = queue.length` before draining the level so children added during the inner loop belong to the *next* level. That boundary is what lets us flip the flag exactly once per level. Everything special about zigzag is layered on top of this standard, well-understood loop.
approaches.insight: Decouple *traversal order* from *output order*. The tree is always walked the same way; a single boolean redirects each value to the front or back of the current row. This separation — 'don't change how you explore, change how you record' — is a reusable principle for any 'same structure, different presentation' problem.

approaches.name: Level-Order BFS Then Reverse Odd Rows
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the simplest-to-explain variant — build normal level order, then reverse every other row. Note the small efficiency cost.
hints: What if you ignore zigzag entirely first, producing plain left-to-right level order?
Once you have the list of rows, which ones are out of order? The odd-indexed levels.
Reverse each odd-indexed row in place at the end. Simpler to reason about, though reversing costs O(width) per odd row.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Standard level-order BFS is O(n). Reversing the odd rows touches each element at most once more → still O(n) total. Output and queue are O(n) / O(w) space.
approaches.explanation:
This variant trades a hair of efficiency for maximum clarity: first produce the ordinary left-to-right level-order traversal, then post-process by reversing every odd-indexed row.

**Why it's the easiest to explain.** Plain level-order BFS is a pattern most people can write without thinking — snapshot the size, drain the level into a list, enqueue children. There's no direction flag to track during traversal, so there's one fewer moving part to get wrong. The zigzag requirement is handled entirely as a separate, obvious cleanup step.

**Why only odd rows are reversed.** The root level (index 0) is already left-to-right, which is correct. Level 1 should be right-to-left, so it needs reversing. Level 2 is correct again, level 3 needs reversing, and so on. The rule is simply: reverse the row when its level index is odd. We can do this inside the loop (reverse before adding when the flag says so) or in a final pass over the result.

**Why it's slightly less efficient than the deque version.** Reversing a row of width `w` is `O(w)` work, and we do it for roughly half the levels. The total extra work is still bounded by `O(n)` across the whole tree, so asymptotically it's identical — but the deque-insertion approach avoids the constant-factor cost of an explicit reversal by placing each value in its final position immediately. In an interview, mentioning that you *know* this difference (same big-O, slightly worse constant) is a nice touch; in practice either is perfectly acceptable.

**Why correctness is obvious here.** Because the traversal is the unmodified, well-trusted level-order routine, the only place a bug could hide is the 'reverse odd rows' step — and that's trivially verifiable. This makes the approach a safe fallback when you want to minimize the chance of an off-by-one or an enqueue-order slip under interview pressure.
approaches.insight: Sometimes the clearest solution is 'solve the simple version, then fix it up'. Producing canonical level order and reversing alternate rows decomposes the problem into two independently-correct pieces, which is often easier to defend than a single cleverer loop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Flipping the child-enqueue order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reversing which child you enqueue first to 'naturally' flip the next level scrambles the order of grandchildren — the corruption compounds down the tree. Keep enqueue order fixed.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Toggling the flag per node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The direction is a property of the LEVEL, not the node. Flipping inside the inner loop alternates within a single row, producing garbage ordering.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: O(width) reversal instead of O(1) front insertion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Building a list then reversing it on every other level repeats work. A deque lets you place each value at its final end in O(1), avoiding the reversal entirely.

patternNote: Level-order BFS with controlled per-level output ordering. Recognise it whenever rows must alternate direction or be presented differently than visited. The lesson — decouple traversal from presentation via a flag and deque-end insertion — generalizes to any serpentine/boustrophedon rendering and to Level Order II's bottom-up flip.
